About this citation

Several letters quote an earlier author — Cleanthes, Hecato, Epicurus — and in those the quoted sentence is that author's, delivered in Seneca's Latin. The archive records the inner attribution in the source field where it is known.

Reading the cited source

The archive attributes this English wording to Letters to Lucilius, Ep. 1 and files it under Stoicism.

What a locator tells you, and what it does not · How this archive traces a quotation

About Seneca

Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BCE–65 CE) was a Cordoban-born Stoic, tragic playwright, and adviser—later forced suicide victim—under Nero.

Interpretation

Seneca opens the Letters with this as the practical conclusion of an argument about time. Most of it, he has said, is taken from us by others or lost to us; the remedy is to gather what remains and keep it. To claim yourself is to stop lending your attention to whatever arrives. The formulation is deliberately economic — he treats time as the one possession that is genuinely ours and therefore the one worth accounting for.

Why it matters

It is a question of ownership: how much of your attention was spent on what you chose, as opposed to what was simply available to be spent?

Questions readers arrive with

What is the source of the quotation “Claim yourself for yourself.”?

“Claim yourself for yourself.” comes from Letters to Lucilius, Ep. 1 (c. 62–65 CE), attributed to Seneca.

What does Seneca mean by autonomy?

Across 4 recurring voices here (notably Seneca and Mary Wollstonecraft), autonomy is framed through Stoicism and Feminist Philosophy. Some passages define autonomy; others warn how it fails; still others relocate it inside habit, community, or language. This passage enters that discussion through autonomy, time, self.
